echoes.note: Stephen opens by calling God 'the God of glory'; the phrase recalls the Psalter's thundering 'God of glory,' lending the divine epiphany to Abraham a cultic-theophanic register from the outset.

'Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you' reproduces the LXX call of Abram almost verbatim — the foundational migration command anchoring the whole speech's theme of God on the move, not bound to one place.
The geography — Mesopotamia, the land of the Chaldeans, settling in Haran before reaching Canaan — tracks Terah's migration from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran exactly; Stephen knows the itinerary.
'When his father was dead, God moved him into this land' presupposes Terah's death at Haran; Stephen harmonizes the chronology around the patriarch's burial there.
Abram's actual departure from Haran into Canaan, the land 'where you are now living,' fulfills the v.3 command and supplies the narrative motion of vv.4.
The promise to give the land 'to him for a possession, and to his seed after him' echoes the first land-grant oath at Shechem 'unto thy seed will I give this land.'
The land given 'for a possession' to Abraham and his seed reproduces the everlasting-possession formula of the covenant chapter, reinforcing that the gift was promissory, not yet realized.

'No inheritance... not so much as to set his foot on' echoes the idiom of 'not so much as a foot breadth' of land — Stephen sharpens the paradox that the promised land yielded Abraham not a single footstep of soil.

'His seed would live as aliens in a strange land, and they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years' is a near-verbatim citation of the covenant-of-the-pieces prophecy of the Egyptian sojourn.
'I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage, and after that will they come out' continues the same Genesis 15 oracle of judgment on the enslaving nation and the exodus.
'And serve me in this place' grafts the burning-bush promise ('ye shall serve God upon this mountain') onto the Genesis 15 prophecy, fusing the two great promises of worship after deliverance.
'He gave him the covenant of circumcision' directly invokes the Genesis 17 institution of circumcision as the sign of the covenant.
Abraham 'circumcised him the eighth day' — Isaac circumcised at eight days old fulfills the eighth-day command and is narrated at Isaac's birth.
'Isaac became the father of Jacob' compresses the generations of Genesis, naming the birth of Jacob to Isaac.
'Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs' alludes to the roster of Jacob's twelve sons, the eponymous ancestors of the tribes.
'The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph' echoes 'his brethren envied him,' the seed of the betrayal — and a deliberate prototype of the present rejection of Jesus.
'Sold him into Egypt' reproduces the brothers selling Joseph to the traders bound for Egypt.
'God was with him' echoes the refrain 'the LORD was with Joseph' that frames his Egyptian career.
Joseph given 'favor and wisdom before Pharaoh' and made 'governor over Egypt and all his house' summarizes Pharaoh's elevation of Joseph over all the land of Egypt.
Joseph made 'ruler of his house, and lord of all his substance' supplies the same poetic summary of his elevation that Stephen's 'governor over... all his house' tracks.
'A famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan' echoes the onset of the seven years of dearth that reached every land.
'Our fathers found no food' reflects the famine 'in the land of Canaan' that drove Jacob's sons to seek grain.
'When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time' reproduces Jacob's command to his sons to go down and buy corn in Egypt.
'On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers' echoes the great recognition scene, 'I am Joseph.'
'Joseph's race was revealed to Pharaoh' echoes the report that reached Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brethren had come.
Joseph 'summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives' reproduces Joseph's message bidding his father come down to him in Egypt.
'Seventy-five souls' follows the Septuagint total of Jacob's household (LXX adds Joseph's grandsons), distinguishing Stephen's source-text from the Hebrew 'seventy.'
The numbering of the household that went down into Egypt (Hebrew 'threescore and ten') is the recurring census tradition Stephen draws on, here in its LXX seventy-five form.
'Jacob went down into Egypt' reproduces the migration of Jacob and all his seed into Egypt.
'And he died' echoes Jacob yielding up the ghost and being gathered to his people.
'Himself and our fathers' died echoes 'Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation,' marking the end of the patriarchal era.
'The tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver' alludes to Abraham's purchase of the field of Machpelah for a burial place — though Stephen telescopes it with the Shechem plot.
The plot 'from the children of Hamor of Shechem' reproduces Jacob's purchase of a parcel at Shechem from the sons of Hamor — Stephen conflates the two patriarchal land purchases.
'Brought back to Shechem' echoes the burial of Joseph's bones in the parcel of ground at Shechem that Jacob bought from Hamor's sons — the source that explains Stephen's Shechem detail.
'The people grew and multiplied in Egypt' reproduces 'the children of Israel were fruitful... and multiplied,' the population explosion that triggers oppression.
'As the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham' loops back to the four-hundred-year covenant prophecy now reaching its term.
'He increased his people greatly' offers the poetic counterpart to Israel's multiplication in Egypt.
'There arose a different king, who didn't know Joseph' is a near-verbatim rendering of 'there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.'
'Took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers' echoes Pharaoh's policy to 'deal wisely' and afflict Israel with burdens.
'Forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn't stay alive' reproduces Pharaoh's edict to cast every newborn son into the river.
Moses 'was exceedingly handsome... nourished three months in his father's house' closely follows 'she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.'
'When he was thrown out' alludes to the mother placing the infant in the ark among the reeds when she could no longer hide him.
'Pharaoh's daughter took him up' reproduces the princess discovering and taking the child from the river.
'Reared him as her own son' echoes 'he became her son' when Moses was brought to Pharaoh's daughter.
'Mighty in his words and works' stands in pointed tension with Moses' own self-description as 'slow of speech'; the haggadic praise of Moses' eloquence amplifies the biblical figure.
'Instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians' presupposes the proverbial 'wisdom of Egypt' that Israel's later tradition both admired and relativized.
Moses, grown, going out 'to visit his brothers, the children of Israel,' reproduces 'Moses... went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens.'
Seeing the wrong and 'striking the Egyptian' reproduces Moses smiting the Egyptian and hiding him in the sand.
'The day following, he appeared to them as they fought' and urged peace reproduces Moses finding two Hebrews striving on the second day.

'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?' is a near-verbatim citation of the rebuffing Hebrew's words — the rejection-of-the-deliverer motif Stephen weaponizes.
'Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian' reproduces Moses fleeing Pharaoh and dwelling in Midian.
Moses becoming 'the father of two sons' in Midian echoes his marriage to Zipporah and the birth of Gershom (the 'stranger in a strange land').
'An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush' reproduces the angel of the LORD in the flame of fire out of the midst of the bush at Horeb.
'Moses... wondered at the sight. As he came close to see' echoes Moses turning aside to see the great sight of the unconsumed bush.
'A voice of the Lord came to him' reproduces God calling to Moses out of the midst of the bush.
'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' is a verbatim citation; 'Moses trembled, and dared not look' reproduces 'Moses hid his face.'

'Take your sandals off of your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground' is a near-verbatim citation — the holy-ground saying that anchors Stephen's argument that God is not confined to the temple.

'I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them' closely follows the LORD's declaration that he has seen the affliction and come down to deliver.
'Now come, I will send you into Egypt' reproduces 'Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh.'
'Heard their groaning' echoes 'God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant,' tying the deliverance to the Abrahamic promise.
'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' is repeated from the Hebrew's taunt, now turned into the structural refrain of Israel rejecting the very deliverer God appoints.
Moses sent 'by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush' loops back to the angel in the burning bush as God's commissioning agent.
'Having worked wonders and signs in Egypt' echoes the LORD multiplying signs and wonders in the land of Egypt through Moses.
Wonders 'in the Red Sea' alludes to the parting of the sea at the exodus.
'In the wilderness for forty years' echoes the forty years of wandering decreed for the rebellious generation.
'The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me' is a verbatim citation of the prophet-like-Moses promise — the christological hinge of the speech.
'In the assembly in the wilderness... on Mount Sinai' alludes to Israel gathered at the foot of Sinai when God spoke.
'Living oracles' (logia zonta) echoes Moses' claim that the law 'is not a vain thing for you; because it is your life' — the Torah as the word of life.
Fathers who 'turned back in their hearts to Egypt' reproduces the wilderness murmuring, 'Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt.'
'Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses... we don't know what has become of him' is a near-verbatim citation of the people's demand to Aaron.
'They made a calf... and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands' reproduces the golden-calf apostasy with its offerings and revelry.
'Rejoiced in the works of their hands' echoes 'they made a calf in Horeb... and changed their glory into the similitude of an ox,' the Psalter's indictment of idolatry.
'Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?' is a direct citation of Amos following the Septuagint.

'You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan... I will carry you away beyond Babylon' cites Amos in its LXX form (Rephan for Hebrew Kiyyun; 'Babylon' for 'Damascus'), turning the exile threat against the temple establishment.
God giving them up 'to serve the army of the sky' echoes the warning against worshipping the host of heaven — the sun, moon, and stars.
Sacrifice 'to the army of the sky' resonates with Jeremiah's denunciation of offerings to the queen of heaven and the host of heaven, the prophetic critique of false worship Stephen invokes.
'The tabernacle of Moloch' resonates with the Levitical prohibition against passing one's seed through the fire to Molech.
The tabernacle made 'according to the pattern that he had seen' cites the command to Moses to make all things after the pattern shown him in the mount.
'The tabernacle of the testimony' echoes the standard Pentateuchal designation 'tabernacle of the testimony' for the wilderness sanctuary.
'Brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations' alludes to Israel crossing Jordan under Joshua to take the land.
'The nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers' echoes the conquest formula that the LORD drove out great nations before Israel.
David 'asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob' alludes to David's wish to build a house for the ark, the occasion of Nathan's oracle.
'A habitation for the God of Jacob' closely follows the Psalmist's vow to 'find out a place... an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob.'
David's desire to house the ark is also recounted in Chronicles, the parallel tradition behind Stephen's compressed summary.
'But Solomon built him a house' reproduces Solomon's construction of the temple, the climax Stephen immediately relativizes.
'The Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands' echoes Solomon's own dedicatory confession, 'the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house?'
'Heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?' is a verbatim citation of Isaiah's oracle against confining God to a temple.
'Didn't my hand make all these things?' continues the Isaiah 66 citation ('all those things hath mine hand made'), grounding the anti-temple argument in the Creator's transcendence.
'You stiff-necked' applies God's own characterization of Israel ('thou art a stiffnecked people') to Stephen's hearers — the post-golden-calf indictment turned on the council.
'Stiff-necked' echoes the repeated Deuteronomic refrain 'thou art a stiffnecked people,' Moses' summary verdict on the wilderness generation.
'Uncircumcised in heart' reproduces the Holiness Code's 'if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled,' the metaphor of inner unfaithfulness.
'Uncircumcised in... ears' echoes Jeremiah's 'their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot hearken' — deaf to the prophetic word.
'You always resist the Holy Spirit' echoes 'they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit' — the rare OT 'Holy Spirit' language Stephen deploys against the present generation.
'Which of the prophets didn't your fathers persecute?' echoes the chronicler's verdict that they 'mocked the messengers of God... and misused his prophets,' the canonical summary of prophet-killing.
'They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One' echoes Elijah's complaint that Israel 'slain thy prophets with the sword.'
'The Righteous One' (ho dikaios) typologically draws on the Servant whom God calls 'my righteous servant,' read as the suffering Messiah.
'You received the law as it was ordained by angels' draws on the LXX of Moses' blessing ('on his right hand... angels with him'), the tradition of angelic mediation of the Sinai law.
Stephen 'saw the glory of God' in opened heaven echoes Ezekiel's vision of 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD,' the prophetic theophany pattern.

Seeing 'Jesus standing on the right hand of God' draws on the enthronement oracle 'Sit thou at my right hand,' the supreme OT proof-text of exaltation — strikingly with Jesus standing rather than seated.
'The Son of Man standing at the right hand of God' fuses Daniel's vision of 'one like the Son of man' coming with the clouds with the right-hand enthronement.
'The witnesses placed their garments' and the stoning reflect the Deuteronomic execution law that 'the hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death.'
Stoning Stephen after the charge of blasphemy against the temple and God reflects the law that 'he that blasphemeth the name of the LORD... all the congregation shall certainly stone him.'
'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!' reworks the Psalmist's 'into thine hand I commit my spirit,' the prayer of the dying righteous now addressed to Jesus.
